full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 13: Outgoing President of the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Chandra Prasad Dhakal, urged the investors of United Arab Emirates to invest in Nepal's hydropower, tourism, agriculture, information technology and data centre.

President Dhakal, who is in UAE to participate in RAK Investment Summit' organised at Ras Al Khaimah of UAE, made this request during the meeting with Minister or Foreign Trade UAE, Dr Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, on Thursday.

On the occasion, they discussed the Nepal-UAE relations, trade expansion and opportunity of available investment in Nepal, according to Dhakal's Private Secretariat.

Appreciating the operation of direct flight from UAE to Pokhara International Airport, Dhakal requested to take initiatives for the operation of direct flight to Bhairahawa-based Gautam Buddha International Airport. (RSS)

title: Nepal's participation in ITU meaningful: Minister Dr Timilsina - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal's participation in ITU meaningful: Minister Dr Timilsina  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 13: Minister for Information and Communications, Dr Bikram Timilsina, has shared that Nepal's participation in the International Telecommunication Union Plenipotentiary Conference (ITU PP-26) was meaningful and effective.

At a news conference organised upon his arrival home at Tribhuvan International Airport today from Qatar after participating in the conference, Minister Dr Timilsina argued that Nepal presented its opinion for reducing 'digital divide' seen in developing countries and increasing access of technology through the use of emerging technology. The ITU PP-26 is underway in Doha of Qatar.

He mentioned that discussions were also held on enhancing cooperation and partnership with the countries, who have achieved remarkable progress in information technology and telecom sector, for digital transformation in coming days.

Stating that bilateral meetings and significant discussions were held with ministers, state ministers of different countries including Malaysia, Estonia, Qatar, China, India and Russia, Minister Dr Timilsina clarified that discussions were held with different countries on the issues of cooperation and partnership in information technology and telecom sectors as per the need and interest of Nepal.

He mentioned that an extensive discussion was held in the conference on how to keep communication system running smoothly during disasters including flood, landslide and earthquake.

In the conference, Minister Dr Timilsina on the behalf of Nepal delivered a speech, emphasizing that the role of communication becomes more effective during disaster hour.

He pointed out the need of targeted technical support, technology transfer and concessional financial assistance to take developing and underdeveloped countries together in the process of digital transformation.

Sharing that a new type of digital divide is being created based on access of emerging technologies including artificial intelligence and 5G along with existing inequality in digital access, Communications Minister Dr Timilsina laid emphasis that international cooperation was indispensable to equally distribute benefits of digital transformation among all countries and communities.

The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) has been working in policy making globally in telecommunication sector. There are 194 member states in ITU. (RSS)

title: Nepalese Hospitals Face Infrastructure Barriers Implementing Digital Antimicrobial Stewardship Programs - Bioengineer.org
description: Nepalese Hospitals Face Infrastructure Barriers Implementing Digital Antimicrobial Stewardship Programs  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
A qualitative exploratory study examining antimicrobial stewardship programs across hospitals in Nepal has identified significant infrastructural and structural barriers that complicate the transition from national policy to practical clinical execution. Researchers investigating the integration of digital health tools within hospital environments found that although awareness of antimicrobial resistance is high among healthcare stakeholders, clinical implementation remains hindered by systemic resource deficits. The inquiry focused on how healthcare facilities can operationalize the country’s National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, underscoring that institutional readiness and technical foundations must be strengthened before digital interventions can effectively assist clinical workflows.

The study was designed around an interpretivist qualitative framework to explore the nuanced perspectives of frontline health system actors. Researchers conducted semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 38 purposively selected participants representing diverse healthcare roles across Nepal. To analyze the qualitative accounts, the investigative team applied Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis methodology, organizing the stakeholder narratives into structured conceptual patterns. The authors reported their methodological procedures in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research checklist, ensuring transparency in their qualitative data collection and analytical synthesis.

Stakeholder interviews revealed four overarching thematic areas that govern stewardship implementation in Nepalese medical facilities. The first theme centered on widespread awareness regarding the urgency of antimicrobial resistance, which participants identified as a severe public health crisis. Contributors noted that the problem is heavily driven by inappropriate prescribing patterns, widespread and unregulated antibiotic access within the broader community, and complex factors spanning human, animal, and environmental domains under a One Health perspective.

The second major theme detailed existing antimicrobial use patterns alongside persistent institutional and systemic deficits. Participants described hospital prescribing as heavily dominated by empirical decision-making, where clinicians frequently select antimicrobials without microbiological guidance. This pattern is compounded by variable adherence to formal clinical guidelines and the operational limitations of hospital antimicrobial stewardship structures, which remain severely constrained by inadequate staffing levels and a lack of formal administrative authority to enforce prescribing policies.

Regarding the integration of digital technology, the third theme evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of electronic tools intended to support antimicrobial stewardship. The interviewees expressed broad overall support for digital solutions, yet highlighted practical concerns surrounding technological fragmentation across hospitals. Institutions exhibited highly variable degrees of digital maturity, and stakeholders consistently emphasized that digital systems must serve solely to aid and support clinical judgment rather than attempting to automate or replace human clinical decision-making.

The final theme synthesized core implementation barriers, facilitators, and strategic recommendations required to achieve sustainable stewardship programs. Key impediments included pervasive healthcare workforce shortages, the absence of interoperability standards between disparate digital platforms, and inconsistent institutional leadership commitment. Participants emphasized that effective execution depends on aligning hospital practices with national health policy and securing sustained long-term investments in human healthcare personnel alongside robust physical and digital technical infrastructure.

The researchers concluded that while basic stewardship structures and diagnostic awareness are already present in several Nepalese facilities, closing the gap between policy and practice demands coordinated systemic intervention across clinical, laboratory, digital, and policy domains. Digital tools offer meaningful support for monitoring and directing antimicrobial utilization, but their practical success relies on addressing foundational prerequisites, including standardized data systems, workforce capacity expansion, and dependable institutional leadership. These empirical findings provide targeted, pillar-specific operational guidance to assist health authorities in executing Nepal’s National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance.

title: Nepal caught in contraband timber stalemate - Nepali Times
description: Nepal caught in contraband timber stalemate  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Over the years, Nepal seized truckloads of the contraband timber being smuggled from India to China. But the red sandalwood is stuck as officials cannot seem to be able to get rid of it.

Under Nepal’s domestic law implementing the Convention on International Trade of Endangered Species (CITES), an international treaty meant to prevent the trafficking of endangered plants and animals, Kathmandu must ask the India to take back confiscated items.

New Delhi has agreed to take back certain amount of the wood, but more than 273 tons of one of the world’s most prized timbers is still sitting in Nepal which does not seem to want to upset its next-door neighbour.

“India is a key ally,” says Maheshwar Dhakal at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest, and Environment. “We worry that putting the timber up for auction could draw criticism from India and strain bilateral relations so Nepal has simply held onto the stock.”

Nepal’s own law says that once the country of origin agrees to take back the confiscated material, it is required to collect it within 90 days and cover the cost of repatriation. If it declines to take back the material or fails to repatriate it within the stipulated period, the law allows Nepal various options: sell the wood by auction, hand it to a public institution for research or religious purposes, or destroy it after approval from local administrative officials.

So far, not one of these options has been taken up by Nepal on the confiscated red sandalwood, ‘red sanders’.

Red sandalwood grows naturally only in a small stretch of southern and eastern India. Prized for its striking red hue and unique medicinal properties, it is used in China to create ornate furniture, musical instruments and even to make traditional remedies.

It is so rare and valuable that it has become one of the most trafficked timbers on the planet, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

ROTTING TIMBER

In 2017, Nepal burned a stockpile of confiscated wildlife parts that it had accumulated for years. But its inventory of seized red sanders is in storage in several places, with some rotting, while at least 19 metric tons have been pilfered.

“Nepal hasn’t put red sandalwood up for auction in over two decades,” says Dhirendra Pradhan at the Department of Forests and Soil Conservation. “That choice rests entirely with the Cabinet – we can’t move forward without a clear mandate, and this lingering uncertainty has turned into a major administrative headache.”

In January 2025, more than 460 kg of red sanders were seized from alleged smugglers in Kathmandu, adding more to the stockpile.

At the Department of Forest and Soil Conservation (DFSC) in Kathmandu, the timber fills seven trucks, their faded, peeling paint revealing years of stagnation. Elsewhere in the country, warehouses at more than 20 divisional forest offices are also full of the smuggled wood.

Since September 2009, 35 police and forest guards have provided round-the-clock security for the red sanders in Kathmandu.

“This is an issue that needs to be resolved,” said Netra Bahadur Karki, of the paramilitary Armed Police Force. “The team could have been deployed elsewhere, but the government is spending resources to guard the red sandalwood. Still, once the state assigns us this responsibility, we have no choice but to carry it out.”

Adhikari, whose responsibilities include ensuring the import and export of endangered species comply with national laws and regulations, worries that more of the stockpile will be stolen, or that its quality will decline.

Nepal’s government has changed 15 times since 2008. The country’s political instability has meant successive administrations did not have enough time to deal with the red sanders stockpile.

“Frequent changes in government have caused the issue to languish,” said Dhakal. “Officials who work on it continuously are often transferred or disconnected from the process. As a result, one government starts the process, but another takes over before it is completed. The new government then has to begin again, leaving Nepal unable to decide on its own.”

title: Nepal Health Professionals Council to Deliver Certificates Home via Mail and Courier - Ratopati
description: Nepal Health Professionals Council to Deliver Certificates Home via Mail and Courier  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. The Nepal Health Professionals Council has put forward a plan to deliver health professionals' certificates to their homes via postal and courier services. The Council has put forward a plan to deliver certificates, letters, and documents to students and service recipients through courier or postal services.

With the objective of making health services more effective, transparent, and technology-friendly, the Council has publicized its major achievements to date and upcoming new annual programs.

For the convenience of service recipients, the Council has established a waiting area and launched a system for registering complaints and suggestions online. Similarly, licensing examinations are regularly conducted to ensure professional competence, and tasks such as handing over aid for the rescue, relief, and rehabilitation of flood and disaster-affected individuals have also been completed.

According to the Council's Chairman Sagun Poudel, the Council has moved forward with various important decisions to systematize legal reforms, regulation, and registration processes. A task force has been formed to collect suggestions to make existing laws timely and inclusive, and the process of amending necessary regulations and laws for governance improvement in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and Food Hygiene has been initiated.

Furthermore, a decision has been made to register MPH, including postgraduate level specializations, and the process of issuing a single certificate for similar subjects like BPH and MPH, instead of separate ones, is also underway. The Council has approved various new programs to strengthen institutional capacity and extend services to doorsteps in the coming days. To encourage research work by students related to health manpower, Student Thesis Grant, arrangement to deliver certificates and documents to doorsteps via postal or courier services, and an integrated system with online renewal and QR code-based identity cards have been launched.

Similarly, interaction programs in all seven provinces, operation of the NHRC HRS Dashboard, and a plan to conduct a paid internship program for health graduates who have recently completed their studies have also been put forward.

On Saturday 14 November, the One Bangkok Forum in Bangkok, Thailand, becomes the centre of Asian music as it hosts the first edition of the Eurovision Song Contest Asia.

With Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop as hosts, it is a historic event bringing together 11 countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. The contest sets out to bring the spirit of the Eurovision format to Asia while showcasing the continent’s cultural, linguistic and musical diversity.

With entrants from different styles, backgrounds and artistic approaches, this first edition aims to become an international showcase for new voices and sounds from one of the most diverse regions on the planet.

(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});

Ahead of the big night, we take a closer look at the careers of the acts competing for victory in a series of profiles dedicated to each participant. We explore their origins, their musical careers, their biggest hits and the stories behind each entry. 11 countries, 11 songs and one stage: Bangkok, where a new chapter in the history of international song contests is about to begin.

This time we meet Pratik Himal Rai, who represents Nepal at Eurovision Asia 2026 with “Ananta Maya” (अनन्त माया), Nepali for Eternal Love .

Who is Pratik Himal Rai? An artist who pours his emotions and experiences into his performances

Pratik Himal Mewahang Rai is a singer, songwriter and performer who will represent Nepal at the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with “Ananta Maya” (अनन्त माया). After more than a decade in music and a career shaped by appearances on several television shows, he won Nepal Decides to become the first Nepalese representative in the history of the Asian contest.

Music has always been the driving force of his artistic journey. A native of Nepal, Pratik Himal Rai has spent more than ten years building his career in his country’s music industry, developing an identity of his own that brings together expressive sensitivity, formal training and an interest in blending musical genres.

His artistry is defined by close attention to emotion and the ability to tell stories through music. As a singer and songwriter, Pratik Himal Rai uses songs as a way to connect with listeners, favouring sincere performances and compositions that reflect his musical personality.

Although he remains relatively little known outside Nepal, his selection for Eurovision Asia 2026 is an important opportunity to bring his work to an international audience and showcase part of the Nepalese music scene.

More than a decade in music

Pratik Himal Rai has more than 10 years of experience in music. Over that time he has worked on his skills as a performer and songwriter, gradually building a career in which versatility is one of his defining traits.

One of the most notable aspects of his profile is his education. Pratik Himal Rai holds a bachelor’s degree in Music, which complements his practical experience and gives him a solid foundation for his creative work. This training allows him to approach his craft from different angles: vocal, interpretative and compositional.

Public recognition came largely through his appearances on television shows, including ‘The Voice of Nepal’. These gave him the chance to show off his vocal skills to wider audiences and prove he could hold a stage.

His emotive voice, expressive sensitivity and stage presence caught viewers’ attention, and his time on television gave him valuable experience in performing on camera and connecting with an audience.

These opportunities have also been part of his growth as an artist, helping him gain experience across different musical formats and raise his profile in Nepalese entertainment.

A musical style that blends tradition and modernity

Pratik Himal Rai‘s musical identity stands out for its diversity. His repertoire spans several genres, including ballads, slow rock , Nepali folk music and folk-pop .

This mix allows him to move between contemporary sounds and elements rooted in his country’s musical traditions. Ballads and slow rock give him room for emotionally charged performances, while folk-pop and traditional influences bring a distinct cultural personality to his songs.

Folk music holds a particularly interesting place in this artistic identity. Nepal has a rich cultural and musical heritage, shaped by the diversity of its communities, languages and traditions. Drawing on folk elements is a way of keeping that heritage alive while exploring new sounds.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pratik Himal Rai (@pratik_himal_rai)

Pratik Himal Rai aims to strike exactly that balance between the traditional and the contemporary. Rather than reproducing set formulas, he seems to be looking for an identity that lets him experiment with different styles without losing the sensitivity that defines his work.

Before his Eurovision Asia entry, the Nepalese singer had released releases including “Chhaina Maile (Live Cover)” in 2025 and “Jhari” (झरी) the following year. In 2026 he also released his first EP, Poetry .

As a songwriter, he places particular emphasis on storytelling and conveying feelings. His songs aim to build an emotional connection with listeners, turning every performance into a chance to share experiences and emotions.

So far, Pratik Himal Rai has two original releases to his name, a catalogue still in the making that reflects an artist who keeps working on new material and looking to grow his presence in the music industry.

Destination Eurovision Asia, his big international project

The next big chapter in Pratik Himal Rai‘s career is his participation in Eurovision Asia 2026. He earned his ticket to the contest’s first edition by winning Nepal Decides, the national selection organised to choose the country’s entry.

Out of 11 competing entries, “Ananta Maya” stood out. His performance won over voters and put him at the top of the scoreboard, giving Pratik Himal Rai the backing he needed to become Nepal’s representative at the new Asian contest.

“Ananta Maya” (अनन्त माया), whose title can be translated as “Infinite Love” or “Eternal Love” , is the song with which he will fly the flag for Nepal in front of an international audience. It gives him the chance to present his musical identity on a much bigger stage, with a song that reflects his artistic sensitivity and his strengths as a performer.

His victory also has a historic dimension for Nepalese music: he will be Nepal‘s first ever representative at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia. For Nepal, his participation is a chance to project its musical culture beyond its borders. The country has a remarkable artistic and cultural diversity, and taking part in a contest like this will introduce some of that richness to new audiences.

Pratik Himal Rai therefore faces a challenge that goes beyond his own development as a singer. His performance will also represent the musical identity of his country, with all the responsibility that comes with it.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Eurovision Song Contest (@eurovision)

A new horizon for his career

Taking part in Eurovision Asia 2026 is one of the most important moments of Pratik Himal Rai‘s career. After more than a decade of work, study and musical experience, he has the chance to raise his profile and present his music to an international audience.

His blend of ballads, slow rock , Nepali folk and folk-pop is a calling card that reflects both his personal interests and his desire to keep a link with his country’s musical roots.

His songwriting also lets him approach this experience from a creative perspective, with songs that aim to convey emotion and build an authentic connection with listeners.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @backyard_by_coffee_club

The stage in Bangkok will be a key showcase for all those years of dedication. With “Ananta Maya”, Pratik Himal Rai will not only perform Nepal‘s first ever entry at Eurovision Asia but also has the chance to open a new chapter in his career.

He is an artist who has built his path through training and television experience, who finds in music a way to tell stories, and who now faces the challenge of taking his voice beyond Nepal’s borders.

“Ananta Maya”: Pratik Himal Rai’s song for Nepal at Eurovision Asia 2026

Pratik Himal Rai represents Nepal at Eurovision Asia 2026 with “Ananta Maya” (अनन्त माया), which translates as “Infinite Love” or “Eternal Love” . The song is sung entirely in Nepali and written by Pratik Himal Rai himself, who uses poetic imagery to describe a love greater than any natural beauty or material limit.

“Ananta Maya” explores the depth of love, its eternal nature and its ability to endure even when everything else is gone.

The lyrics open by evoking the vastness of the ocean, the expanse of the blue sky and landscapes that seem to go on forever. Yet the narrator says that his love for the person he loves is greater still. The comparison conveys that what he feels cannot be measured in physical terms, because it surpasses even the most awe-inspiring dimensions of nature.

One of the most striking passages is the chorus, which repeats that even if all things cease to exist, his love will not disappear. It also uses the image of ashes after a fire to say that even when everything has burned and turned to dust, the feeling will live on: a metaphor for love’s endurance in the face of time, destruction and change.

Elsewhere, the song turns to images of light, silence and calm. The light and golden tones of a peaceful evening represent the beauty of the world, but the singer finds his love brighter and more colourful than any landscape. The loved one thus becomes the centre of an emotional experience that gives meaning and beauty to everything around.

Ultimately, “Ananta Maya” is a celebration of unconditional, deep and eternal love. Its message is that true love does not depend on circumstances, appearances or the permanence of material things. Even when the world changes or disappears, genuine feeling remains. Through simple, symbolic and deeply romantic language, Pratik Himal Rai delivers a declaration of love that aspires to be as infinite as the universe itself.

Pratik Himal Rai represents Nepal at the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia after winning Nepal Decides with “Ananta Maya” (अनन्त माया).

Nepal Decides, organised by Nepalese broadcaster Himalaya TV, used a mixed voting system to choose the country’s representative for the first edition of Eurovision Asia. The national final, held on Wednesday 7 October, was hosted by Roneeshma Shrestha, one of the most popular faces on Nepalese television, and produced by Himalaya TV in collaboration with Voxovation.

Pokhara — Framed by the snow-capped Annapurna range, Phewa Lake is the beating heart of Pokhara’s identity and its tourism economy. Yet, beneath its postcard-perfect surface, this vital freshwater ecosystem is fighting a silent battle against a relentless tide of plastic. Every monsoon, feeder streams like the Firke Khola wash tons of household plastics and discarded packaging directly into the lake. While local community groups have long led tireless weekend clean-ups, scooping plastic out of open waters is a grueling, endless race.

Photo: UNDP Nepal

Now, a simple yet highly innovative preventive solution is turning the tide—intercepting plastic pollution directly at the source and transforming waste into a valuable resource. Intercepting waste before it reaches the lake Two floating waste traps have been installed at key locations along the waterways entering Phewa Lake. The first installation featuring eight modular units is at the confluence of Bulaudi Khola and Firke Khola, behind the Baidam Police Office, covering Wards 6 and 17. The second, with seven floating units, is located near Annapurna Basic School, along the Annapurna School corridor, covering Wards 6 and 7.

Photo: UNDP Nepal

Installed diagonally across rushing streams, they intercept and collect floating debris, guiding it safely toward designated riverbank recovery points while allowing clean water and natural sediment to flow harmlessly underneath. Secured by high-tensile steel cables and heavy-duty concrete anchors, these structures are built to withstand the elements. Crucially, local caretakers and municipal personnel have been fully trained and equipped with safety gear to ensure the booms are regularly monitored and cleared. Circular economy in action: Waste as a resource What makes this initiative uniquely UNDP is its commitment to the circular economy.

Photo: UNDP Nepal

Beyond preventing plastic pollution, the initiative demonstrates how discarded materials can be repurposed to address environmental challenges. Recovered PET bottles have been incorporated into the floating boom structures, illustrating how materials commonly regarded as waste can be transformed into practical solutions.

title: Nepal retains 'BB-' rating despite rising debt and flood damage - MorungExpress
description: Nepal retains 'BB-' rating despite rising debt and flood damage  MorungExpress
publisher.title: MorungExpress
full_article:
Kathmandu, November 13 (IANS): Nepal has retained a 'BB-' sovereign credit rating from Fitch Ratings, with the agency citing the country's low public and external debt, strong foreign exchange reserves and robust remittance inflows. This is the third consecutive year Nepal's sovereign credit rating has remained unchanged since it received its first-ever sovereign rating in 2024.

In its latest rating report, the international credit rating agency said Nepal's rating was supported by low government and external debt, mostly on highly concessional terms, strong external liquidity and access to multilateral financing.

Nepal's solid medium-term growth prospects, underpinned by investment in hydropower development, were also cited as supporting factors.

"The ratings are constrained by an underdeveloped economy that is vulnerable to external shocks and natural disasters," Fitch said. "Structural features, such as GDP per capita and governance metrics, are also weaker than those of 'BB' category peers."

Despite a substantial increase in Nepal's public debt, both domestic and external, over the past decade since the devastating earthquake of 2015, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have continued to classify the country's debt distress risk as low.

As of the first quarter of the current fiscal year 2026-27, which began in mid-July, Nepal's public debt surpassed NPR 3 trillion for the first time, reflecting a rapid increase in the Himalayan country's debt burden over the past decade, the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) of Nepal said.

The government's total outstanding debt reached NPR 3,009 billion, equivalent to 45.59 percent of GDP, compared with NPR 697.68 billion, or 26.84 percent of GDP, in fiscal year 2016-17.

Fitch said Nepal's external debt was highly concessional, with solid prospects for official creditor support.

"This structure preserved financing flexibility amid the shocks from the September 2025 youth-led protest and the August 2026 floods and is further reinforced by the successful completion of Nepal's IMF programme in June 2026," it said.

Fitch said Nepal's economic growth was projected to slow in the current fiscal year 2026-27 due to the impact of the devastating floods of August 26.

The floods killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The disaster also caused substantial economic losses, with physical damage estimated at 1.66 billion U.S. dollars, according to the World Bank.

"The August 2026 flash floods, which caused substantial human and economic losses, will weigh on near-term growth," Fitch said. "The floods affected more than 10 percent of the country's installed power capacity and disrupted electricity generation and transmission, transport connectivity, tourism and industrial activity. Restoration and reconstruction efforts will support the economic recovery."

Fitch projected Nepal's economic growth to slow to 3.4 percent in FY2026-27, down from 3.9 percent in FY2025-26, citing the impact of the August floods.

The international rating agency also expects economic growth to rebound to 5.2 percent in FY2027-28, supported by accelerated reconstruction activities and the restoration of hydropower projects and electricity-grid infrastructure.

"However, delays in reconstruction and a prolonged conflict involving Iran could further undermine growth prospects by disrupting energy and fertiliser imports, increasing supply risks and affecting tourism receipts," it said.

The rating agency also noted that Nepal had an opportunity to improve policy predictability and advance economic reforms following the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party's clear parliamentary majority in the March elections.

"The party has set out a near-term reform agenda to improve governance and the business climate, although the floods could complicate the balance between reform priorities and immediate emergency relief," Fitch said. "Political instability could re-emerge if the ruling party fails to deliver credible reforms or relies excessively on ordinances to implement policy."

title: How Nepal’s tile makers have gained ground against Chinese and Indian imports - The Kathmandu Post
description: How Nepal’s tile makers have gained ground against Chinese and Indian imports  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Tile Wars, a Spain-based publication covering the global ceramic tile industry, has published an analysis of Nepal’s ceramic tile sector, examining how domestic manufacturers have established a presence in a market long dominated by imports from China and India.

The analysis looks at how manufacturers in landlocked Nepal have competed with large-scale Chinese producers and low-cost factories in Morbi, a ceramic manufacturing hub in Gujarat, India.

It features Lumbini Ceramics, which produces fully vitrified tiles under the Laminar brand at its factory in Gulariya, Bardiya. The company has also started exporting tiles to Uttar Pradesh in India.

Shorter delivery times have helped domestic manufacturers compete with imported products, the publication says. Imported tiles must cross the border and clear customs, while local producers can replenish stocks more quickly when retailers place new orders or contractors need additional tiles of the same design to complete projects.

Product certification has also helped build confidence in locally manufactured tiles. The Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology has certified Laminar as fully vitrified and Lumbini Ceramics’ Cresta line as porcelain under NS 617:2082.

The bureau's certification register also lists Prime Ceramics in Rautahat and Kajaria Ramesh Tiles in Nawalparasi under the ceramic tile standard.

Lumbini Ceramics managing director Ashutosh Khetan told the Post that imports from India once accounted for nearly 99 percent of Nepal's tile demand. He estimated that imports now make up around 20 percent of the market, while his company's share of domestic sales stands at about 25 percent.

The Gulariya factory uses digital printing technology to apply designs to tile surfaces. The company sources printing ink from Spain and glaze from Italy.

Antalya (Turkiye), Nov 13: Nepal has sought Chinese support for the establishment of the proposed Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism under the leadership of Nepal, India and China.

Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment, Gita Chaudhary, put forth such proposal in a bilateral meeting with Chinese Minister of Ecology and Environment, Huang Runqiu, here Thursday. The meeting was held on the sideline of COP31, which is going on here since November 9.

Minister Chaudhary reminded that Himalayan region was facing increasing risk due to climate change, which is a common trans-boundary challenge. It requires regional cooperation to address this crisis, according to Minister Chaudhary's Secretariat.

title: Nepal’s climate suffering must pave the way for a safe and fair future - Climate Home News
description: Nepal’s climate suffering must pave the way for a safe and fair future  Climate Home News
publisher.title: Climate Home News
full_article:
Gita Chaudhary is Nepal's Minister of Agriculture, Forests and Environment .

We are still grieving the thousands dead and missing from the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi climate catastrophe on August 26. The ice-rock avalanche originated at 5,200m above sea level and carried roughly 100 million cubic metres of debris-laden water, at an average speed of 150km/h, burying homes, farms, schools in minutes. We lost more than 1,400 lives and more than 5,200 people remain missing.

Scientists have classified 21 glacial lakes in Nepal as dangerous due to melting permafrost and ice in the Himalayas, so even as we work on the recovery, we believe this can happen again.

Heavy rain in late September and again in October has caused further deadly avalanches, landslides and flooding, adding to people’s pain.

The "roof" of the world - mountain top glaciers that more than 1.9 billion people rely on for water and energy - is no longer stable.

New conversation on climate justice

I represent a young nation. Our administration was elected into office by young people who want transparency and accountability in politics, just like their peers around the world.

In addition to the massive challenges our administration now faces - it will cost at least 10% of our GDP to respond to the glacial collapse - we are committed to building a state that delivers decent jobs, social protection, and a fair chance for every Nepali to thrive at home.

This is why we also believe in multilateralism. We are ready to lead a new conversation about climate justice in today’s context, shaped by the aspirations of a new generation.

Nepal seeks stronger recognition of mountain issues in UN climate process

We may be at the sharp edge of the climate crisis, but the whole world is in this together. The impacts we now face are precisely what the international agreements on climate change were designed to protect against. The science was clear this would happen. That’s why the world agreed over ten years ago, together, to limit warming to 1.5ºC - to avoid dangerous climate change.

Solidarity for one another was at the heart of those agreements, along with the "common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities" principle that those who have historically contributed more to the problem, and those with greater capacity to respond, must do more.

Push for formal recognition at COP

In the mountains, the climate crisis arrives early. This is why Nepal has proposed a new Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, and why we joined with the Royal Government of Bhutan, and the government of Kyrgyzstan to push for COP31 to formally recognise the challenge mountains are facing with a standalone agenda item in Antalya. We urgently need to discuss with the international community how we can better access finance that is adequate, timely, accessible, predictable and grant-based, as well as support for research and early warning systems.

Nepal and Bhutan's submitted agenda will now be further discussed at the COP presidency consultation, where we have also highlighted that the mountain framework should be focused and reflected in the cover decision. This week and next we will be engaging with governments and the COP presidency for the mountain agenda. Progress in these dialogues is essential.

Nepal's member of parliament Sagar Dhakal speaks next to activist Greta Thunberg on day four at the COP31 UNFCCC Climate Conference on November 12, 2026 in Antalya, Turkey. (Photo: Burak Kara/Getty Images) Nepal's member of parliament Sagar Dhakal speaks next to activist Greta Thunberg on day four at the COP31 UNFCCC Climate Conference on November 12, 2026 in Antalya, Turkey. (Photo: Burak Kara/Getty Images)

Meanwhile, we are deeply grateful for the support of our neighbours and other friendly countries who came to our immediate aid in August. Individuals and companies from all over the world have donated to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, touching our hearts when they are most tender.

Solidarity and friendships you can count on are essential when disaster comes to your door.

And every door is at risk. Climate-charged floods, wildfires and droughts that destroy lives and livelihoods and affect supply chains across borders are here to stay.

Funding and technology needed

This is why it’s more critical than ever that dedicated, predictable, adequate, accessible grant-based funding is available, fast and fair to help people cope with the loss and damage now, and adapt to what is coming and build community resilience.

We also need to see clear, actionable roadmaps for transitioning away from fossil fuels, aligned with the 1.5ºC temperature limit, with clear timelines, and protections for workers and communities, as the UN Secretary-General recently called for in New York.

Loss and damage fund agrees $20m for Nepal but rich nations warn it should not set precedent

Last year the International Court of Justice reinforced the fact that all nation-states have strict legal obligations under international law to protect the climate system and curb greenhouse gas emissions.

In Nepal, we see great potential for revolutionary developments in information and power to drive down emissions and support new state-of-the-art solutions to the climate crisis. These could include sophisticated yet easily accessible early warning systems that save lives and livelihoods.

We may not be able to put the roof of the world back together by ourselves, but with solidarity from the global community, in the spirit of multilateralism, we can look at new ways of building the future for the safety and security of us all.

title: Hicksville brothers hope changing brand of Glen Cove Nepali eatery boosts business - Newsday
description: Hicksville brothers hope changing brand of Glen Cove Nepali eatery boosts business  Newsday
publisher.title: Newsday
full_article:
As brothers Bikash and Parash Kharel worked to introduce Glen Cove to Nepali cuisine, a customer base largely unfamiliar with the food, along with rising tariffs, left them in a difficult position just two years after opening their restaurant.

They had brought While in Kathmandu, renamed Delhi to Kathmandu in August, to Glen Cove in 2024 after years of success at the original location in Ridgewood, Queens.

When the eatery opened on Glen Street, Bikash Kharel, 32, of Hicksville, said he envisioned that at least a third of its clientele would be young adults and college students. But they didn't show up in the numbers he had anticipated.

Parash Kharel, 37, also of Hicksville, said he and his brother, both born in Nepal, fell in love with Glen Cove on childhood fishing trips and had hoped to re-create the lively atmosphere of the Ridgewood establishment, where twentysomethings often fill the bar seats.

"In the initial phases, we definitely saw good local reception ... but we experienced that it was an older eating group ... and their palate, with our food, was not the best match," said Bikash Kharel, referencing both the spiciness of their dishes and an unfamiliarity with Nepali cuisine as the reasons.

Tariffs take a toll

President Donald Trump's new tariffs on imported products in 2025 exacerbated the issue.

Month after month, tariffs on key ingredients imported from Nepal, like fermented leafy greens called gundruk, and low foot traffic at the restaurant started to weigh on them. After labor and operating costs, Parash Kharel said, the eatery was barely profitable.

He began to ask himself if the restaurant was worth the sacrifice.

But their father, Bed P. Kharel, pushed the brothers. After immigrating to the United States from Nepal in 2001, the elder Kharel worked at an Indian restaurant. Bikash Kharel said this was common among Nepali immigrants at the time.

Eventually, their father opened his own Indian restaurants, one in Ridgewood on the same street where Bikash Kharel would open While in Kathmandu, with his brother soon joining him.

"The thing about being a small-business owner, you can never give up. I mean, that's something our daddy instilled in us. ... If something doesn't work out, try another way," Parash Kharel said.

So he leaned into adjusting to the Glen Cove market, bringing live jazz on Friday nights and decreasing the spice level of the food based on each customer’s preference.

Bestsellers after rebranding

In August, the duo rebranded the entire spot to an Indian-Nepali fusion restaurant with a new menu and name. One bestseller has been a Nepali staple called momos, which are dumplings, with an option to add Indian butter sauce — an American favorite often paired with chicken.

"Water buffalo momo is something that is more than comfort to us. When we're kids, especially my generation, we used to get a couple of bucks to go to lunch. You could get a water buffalo momo with jhol," Parash Kharel explained. Jhol is a savory soup. "Every day I'm pretty much retelling the whole story again and again."

The business issues weren’t unique to the Kharel brothers' establishment.

Before Delhi to Kathmandu, the space had been occupied by an Indian restaurant called Tava, which opened in 2021 and closed in 2024. Right next door at 63 Glen St., Parash has seen three restaurants come and go: a Thai restaurant named Thaiana, a fast-casual Asian eatery called Coo Coo Kitchen and most recently a Hawaiian restaurant called Lulu Hawaii.

Even at the Ridgewood location, things are changing.

When Bikash Kharel opened While in Kathmandu in 2017, he said, Ridgewood was in the early stages of gentrification, which was initially great for business. But as the neighborhood continued to evolve, he began to worry about the restaurant becoming a "has-been."

It's leaning into Ridgewood’s new fine dining landscape with dishes like lamb chop braised with chhyang, which is a sweet, tangy, mildly alcoholic fermented grain. The entree is served with tomatoes and a wild perilla seed called silam on traditional bronze plates called chares.

"We’re using primarily Nepali ingredients to showcase a dish that is already readily popular in the American marketplace ... using both sides of where I come from and where I am," Bikash Kharel said. The new Ridgewood menu debuts later this month.

Parash Kharel said he has seen more foot traffic after changing the menu but still has concerns.

"We're doing good, but then again doing good business and being profitable is another thing ... just making enough to pay the bills," he said.

Realistically, it would help to raise prices. While customers were understanding of that decision in Ridgewood, Parash Kharel added, it would be less welcome in Glen Cove. With a faltering economy, he said, even regulars who used to frequent the restaurant several times a month told him they can’t afford to come in as often anymore.

"We are looking for a solution, but we're also hoping it'll pass," he said. "It's not only me, as a small business, hurting. I think it's the everyday people. Everyday folks are hurting, too."

Newsday's Erica Marcus contributed to this story.

title: Nepali climate activists appeal for urgent action at COP31 | NHK WORLD-JAPAN News - NHKニュース
description: Nepali climate activists appeal for urgent action at COP31 | NHK WORLD-JAPAN News  NHKニュース
publisher.title: NHKニュース
full_article:
An environmental group from Nepal has appealed for cross-border cooperation on disasters at COP31, the UN climate change conference, in Turkey. An area along the Nepal-China border was devastated by mudslides in August.

The group of mostly young climate activists hosted an event at the COP31 venue on Wednesday.

The group's leader, Dikshya Subedi, spoke about the mudslide disaster. Her relatives are among the survivors. Subedi said the disaster highlighted problems with climate justice. She said this discussion is very important because countries and communities that have contributed the very least to climate change are facing similar disasters every year.

People from Nepal's neighbors, such as India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, attended the event. They discussed ways to procure funds to cover losses from climate-linked disasters and compensation, and to establish a system for data-sharing and early warnings. The participants confirmed the need for countries affected by climate change to step up cooperation.

A woman from Bhutan said it's good that the people of Nepal want to take action. She expressed hope they can unite, put up a stronger front and demand climate justice and climate finance in a fair form.

Subedi also said regional cooperation is necessary because climate change has no borders. She said this time it was Nepal, but the next time it could be another country. She called for urgent preparations, saying the climate crisis is already here and there is no time left.
